description:
Every Signal Matters. Every Astronaut Counts.
In space, every heartbeat tells a story. ZERO G HEALTH is an innovative health-monitoring software concept designed to track astronauts’ vital signs, detect changes in their health, and turn real-time data into actionable insights. Because when humans explore beyond Earth, protecting their health is just as important as reaching the stars.
summary: Zero G Health is an offline-first health monitoring prototype for crews on long missions, such as a Mars transit, where messages to Earth can take about 20 minutes and links can drop completely. Instead of comparing every astronaut with population thresholds, it learns each person's own baseline for six indicators (resting heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep, radiation dose rate, PVT-B vigilance lapses and mood) and flags when someone stops behaving as usual. Every alert explains what changed, by how much, how it was detected and which conservative follow-up is suggested, and serious alerts are routed to the crew medical officer. A reproducible simulator injects known health events so the method can be tested honestly: on 40 held-out simulated missions, the personal-baseline Act level detected 98.9% of events with 0.78 false-alarm episodes per 30 astronaut-days, versus 88.9% and 1.87 for a fixed population threshold. The tool also shows where personalization does not help. Everything runs locally with no Internet. All data are simulated, and it is an educational prototype, not a medical device.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Zero G Health monitors the health of a small crew without depending on Earth. For each of four fictional astronauts it tracks six indicators: resting heart rate, heart rate variability (RMSSD), sleep duration, daily radiation dose rate, a 3-minute PVT-B vigilance test (lapses and false starts) and a one-minute daily mood check-in. Each day, every value is compared with that person's own baseline: the median of their previous 14 valid days, scaled by a robust spread (1.4826 x MAD). Today's value and past alert days never enter the baseline, so a slow deterioration is not "normalized". Levels are Watch (repeat the measurement) and Act (notify the Medical Officer), with persistence rules for slow changes.

Every alert answers five questions: what changed, by how much, how it was detected, what follow-up is suggested and which source supports it. Recommendations are conservative follow-up steps only; the system never diagnoses or suggests medication. The Medical Officer can acknowledge, postpone, escalate or resolve each alert, with a note. A delayed-link layer models the communication delay to Earth and a blackout window; during a blackout, detection keeps running on board and reports wait in a local queue until the link returns.

HOW WE TESTED IT

A seeded mission simulator injects known events (progressive fatigue, physiological stress, a solar particle event, behavioral change, missing data). The cutoffs were tuned on one set of simulated missions and evaluated on a separate set of 40 missions (279 events). The personal-baseline Act level detected 98.9% of events with 0.78 false-alarm episodes per 30 astronaut-days; a fixed population reference range detected 88.9% with 1.87. We also report where we do not win: the fixed threshold alerts earlier on large or fast changes, and with very homogeneous crews personalization gives no advantage. Everything is reproducible and visible in the Validation Lab.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Crews on deep-space missions will need to detect gradual health changes in themselves when real-time support from Earth is limited. A personal baseline can notice a change that is normal for one person but not for another. The intended impact is earlier, explained, low-burden awareness for the crew and the medical officer, plus a transparent way to compare detection methods before any real use.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, SQLite, NumPy/pandas and pytest on the backend; Vue 3, Vite, Pinia, Vue Router, ECharts and a service worker (PWA) on the front end. It runs locally on a laptop or tablet with no cloud services and no API keys. A public demo is hosted for reviewers.

LIMITATIONS

All measurements, crew members, events, blackout and transmissions are simulated. There is no clinical validation and no real astronaut data. Recommendations are illustrative and need medical review. The code can ingest real data from CSV, which is the next step.

SUPERINTELLIGENCE (SI) DISCLOSURE

We used Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, as a tool to accelerate development. It helped write and review the source code (backend, front end and tests), draft documentation and interface text, and generate the four illustrated portraits of the fictional crew (vector SVG), which are labeled "AI-generated" in the app. The demo data are synthetic and generated by the project's own seeded simulator. The team defined the problem, made the design decisions, ran and reviewed the results, and is responsible for the content. No audio or video was generated by SI. The videos and the Earth and Mars images are NASA public-domain media. The project does not use, contain or modify any NASA branding.
